name: Urama
confidence_why: Brown, Muir, Craig and Anea (2016) describe Urama word prosody as a tonal accent with at most one high tone per word and no fixed stress, and the Kope studies by Petterson (2022) and Martin (2016) likewise find word-level pitch melodies rather than fixed or lexical stress, differing only on whether the system is better called tone or pitch accent.
catalog_citation: Brown, Jason, Alex Muir, Kimberley Craig & Karika Anea. 2016. A short grammar of Urama. (Asia-Pacific Linguistics 32.) Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics, ANU. 143 pp. hdl:1885/111328. Open-access ANU repository PDF re-opened in our copy: the copy we hold, text layer.
catalog_locator: Chapter 2 'Phonology', sec.4 'Suprasegmental phonology', 4.1 'Tonal accents', pp.14-15 (PDF pp.23-24; text layer); also p.8 sec.1 Introduction (text).
catalog_quote: Urama makes use of a sophisticated system of tonal accents. There are few minimal pairs that contrast tonally, though the nature of the contrasts is indicative of the larger effect that tone has in the language. The few minimal pairs6 that contrast with respect to tone are given in (16): (16) Surface contrasts in pitch [nimo] ‘us’ LH [nimo] ‘lice’ LL. Given the sparse number of minimal tone pairs, and given that they are all disyllabic, this suggests that the tonal patterns in the language are not contrastive, but rather constitute a tonal accent. This analysis is along the lines of that proposed by Donohue (1997) for the related Northeastern Kiwaian language Arigibi. Donohue claims that the constraints on tonal melodies consist of the following restrictions: (i) every word must have a L tone, and (ii) every word may have a H tone. [...] Note that words can only have a single H tone, but that a H tone is not necessary (cf. monosyllabic words, where the condition cannot apply, as per condition (i) above). Therefore, words must have at least one L tone, but can have a single H accent (on any syllable). The presence of the tonal accent in Urama has been argued by Wurm (1951) to be the result of diachronic processes that have eliminated consonants.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Urama (Northeast Kiwai) word prosody is a culminative tonal (pitch) accent, not stress: a word carries at most one H-toned (accented) syllable, whose position is lexically specified and may be any syllable of the word; words may also be accentless (all L). No rule assigning prominence to a fixed position is given, and the grammar makes no separate statement about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables cannot satisfy the 'at least one L' condition when H (noted by the authors); a few apparent minimal pairs may instead involve vowel length, which the authors regard as idiosyncratic since there is no true length contrast (fn.6). For the Kope dialect, Martin 2016:66 finds instead that every word has at least one H syllable, and Clifton 1986:7 notes that 'stress and tone seem tied together' with lexically placed prominence (['oobo] 'woman' vs [o'bo] 'water').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level melodies established on citation forms and cognate lists (Arigibi/Urama pairs); sec.4.2 separately treats phrase intonation (falling declaratives, nuclear accent on the predicate in yes/no questions). Wurm 1973:250 and Martin 2016:67 both state explicitly that stress in North-Eastern Kiwai has not yet been studied.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Urama dialect (Glottolog uram1241) of Northeast Kiwai. Supporting first-hand remarks on the Kope/Gope dialect (kope1239) come from Clifton 1986 and Martin 2016; Donohue 1997 (not opened) treats Arigibi/Anigibi (arig1248); Wurm 1973 gives examples from Gibaio (giba1246) and Urama. Glottolog's top-ranked 'grammar' for nort2930, Ray 1933, is per Wurm 1973:219 a grammar of Island Kiwai (Southern Kiwai, sout2949), not of Northeast Kiwai. Note the dialects differ in detail: Urama words may be accentless (at most one H), whereas Martin finds every Kope word has at least one H syllable.

new_statements.quote: p.233: “it is good to codify how stress is assigned, as the two phenomena are clearly related. This is done in (6), which also covers the fact that stress is not perceived on words of /HH/ and /LH/ tone patterns when they are spoken in isolation.” p.234: “(6) Isolation Stress a. With words of a single tone pattern pronounced in isolation, stress is assigned to any syllable containing a non-final peak in pitch. b. With /LH-LH/ tone pattern words, stress is assigned to the first syllable of each component pattern as a common alternative to subrule (a).” p.272: “It is clear that stress … and tone interact in Kope, but a careful study of this interaction is beyond the scope of this paper.”

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog's only statement (Brown et al. 2016, Urama) reads the language as a tonal/pitch accent with sparse disyllabic minimal pairs. Petterson's Kope analysis differs in type: four contrastive morpheme-level tone melodies including a three-tone /LHL/, with the mora as TBU and extensive tone sandhi, i.e. a tone system, with stress a derived, non-contrastive by-product of pitch peaks and moraic rhythm; he does not call it pitch accent (Schulz p.12 reports Martin 2016 left that question open). Placement-wise it is compatible with the catalog's empty rule field: there is no fixed stress position. Note the two works describe different NE Kiwai dialects (Kope vs Urama), so part of the disagre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kope (a NE Kiwai dialect) is a tone language: the mora is the tone-bearing unit and four contrastive underlying tone patterns, /HH/ level, /HL/ falling, /LH/ rising and /LHL/ peaking, belong to whole morphemes (p.223); no */LL/ or */HLH/ nouns exist (p.231). Stress (defined in fn.7, p.233, as loudness prominence) is not lexical but derived: in isolation it falls on the syllable carrying a non-final pitch peak, so /HL/ words are initial-stressed ([ˈdúò] 'night', [ˈdódōɾò] 'river bank'), /LHL/ words are stressed on the H syllable ([ɡēˈɾóʔò] 'rat', [ɡōʔāˈɡōóʔà] 'frog'), and /HH/ and /LH/ words carry no perceived stress ([kákápí] 'finger', [kēbāɾí] 'tusk'); compound /LH-LH/ words stress the first syllable of each component (pp.231-234). In phrases stress is governed by ranked constraints (§12.11, pp.272-273): (i) a short syllable cannot be stressed before another stressed syllable; (ii) an initial high-toned syllable attracts stress; (iii) a rhythm with a beat on alternate moras is preferred, so heavy (2-mora) syllables tend to attract stress; (iv) stress is attracted to a high surface tone rather than a low one; and stress is stronger near the phrase's pitch peak. Schulz (p.12) notes Martin (2016) left open 'whether it is better described as a pitch accent language'; Petterson does not adopt a pitch accent analysis.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary (weaker) stress is transcribed with ˌ on syllables away from the phrase's pitch peak, e.g. [ˈɡēɾóˈʔōī ˌkà] 'it is the rat' (p.273); the declarative clitic kaHL 'often sounds like it has a light stress' and 'there is always a degree of stress on kaHL' (pp.241, 266), whereas the interrogative clitic raLL and agentive roLL 'never seem to receive a stress, not even a secondary one' (p.279). Focus lowers pitch and weakens stress on non-focused words (p.286).
new_statements.exceptions: idomaiLH2 'eye' has stress on syllables 1 and 3 for most speakers but one speaker stresses only the peak (second) syllable (p.231); adding the article -i shifts stress from the first to the second syllable of the noun (umu kaa vs umui kaa) and for umai kaa, umuu kaa the stress becomes 'even' over the whole word, shown with parentheses (pp.272-273, 279-281); in bia-phrases kebariLH and kakapiHH show second-syllable stress with no pitch peak, attributed to alternating-mora rhythm (p.264). The author states the stress rules are provisional, OT-style constraints, not a complete account (pp.272, 290). Part I-II (Schulz's grammar) has no phonology chapter and says 'tonal research is not within the reach of this study' (p.42); ch. 11 notes the habitual -ika vs declarative -i=ka homonyms differ in tone and stress on /ka/ (p.193).
new_statements.identity_note: Studies in Kope describes Kope, one of the five NE Kiwai tribal dialects (Anigibi, Kope, Gibaio, Fomomoto/Era, Urama; Schulz pp.8-10), with data mainly from Samson Aumarie of Ubuo village and Ikupu Gigimai of Bavi (p.223); the catalog's existing statement is for the Urama dialect (Brown et al. 2016, Auckland-based speakers). Both fall under Glottolog nort2930 (Northeast Kiwai [kiw]); the catalog label 'Urama' names only one of these varieties.

readall_conflicts: Brown, Muir, Craig & Anea (2016, Urama) treat the pitch contrasts as a non-contrastive tonal accent along the lines of Donohue (1997), while Petterson (2022, Kope, ch. 12) posits four contrastive underlying tone patterns per morpheme (/HH/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/) with the mora as tone-bearing unit and derives stress from surface pitch peaks plus an alternating-mora rhythm, never adopting the pitch accent label; Schulz (2022:12) records that Martin (2016) explicitly left open whether Kope 'is better described as a pitch accent language'. The disagreement is one of analysis (word-tone/melody system vs. tonal accent) and possibly of dialect (Kope vs. Urama, two of the five NE Kiwai varieties under nort2930); on stress placement there is no conflict, since both agree stress is not lexically fixed. Petterson himself flags his stress account as a provisional, incomplete constraint ranking (pp.272, 290).

sources.note: Kope dialect, sec.5 p.7: 'Kope clearly distinguishes vowel length and/or stress or tone', with minimal pairs transcribed with stress marks on different syllables (['abea] 'father' vs [a'beea] 'sago squeezing bag'; ['oobo] 'woman' vs [o'bo] 'water'; [tu'tuu] 'long' vs ['tutu] 'handle'); 'stress and tone seem tied together'; speakers describe the contrast as 'stretch'. No positional rule; contrast is lexical.
